facts.statement: Vegavis notopothousa was described by Irazoqui and colleagues.
Vegavis notopothousa lived during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Maastrichtian stage.
The type locality for Vegavis notopothousa is the López de Bertodano Formation.
facts.quote: Type locality: López de Bertodano Formation

facts.statement: Fossils of Vegavis notopothousa have been found in Antarctica.
Vegavis notopothousa is classified as a neornithine and is a species within the genus Vegavis.
facts.quote: Notes: A neornithine; a species of Vegavis.

facts.statement: Vegavis notopothousa was formally described as a new species in 2026.
facts.quote: In 2026, Irazoqui and colleagues described this specimen as the holotype of a new species of Vegavis, named V. notopothousa.

facts.statement: The specific name 'notopothousa' combines Greek words meaning 'south' and 'longing', referencing the fossil's discovery in the Southern Hemisphere and current housing in the Northern Hemisphere.
facts.quote: The specific name combines the Greek words nótos, meaning south and póthos, referring to longing, alluding to the discovery of the holotype in the Southern Hemisphere but now housed in the Northern Hemisphere.

facts.statement: The geological unit containing Vegavis notopothousa fossils is dated to approximately 69.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: The Sandwich Bluff Member (unit klb 1) of the Lopez de Bertodano Formation on Vega Island, the type locality of V. iaai and V. notopothousa, is dated to the middle Maastrichtian, approximately 69.2 million years ago.

facts.statement: Vegavis possessed a high metabolism that enabled it to survive in the high latitudes of Antarctica.
facts.quote: Vegavis was a bird with a high metabolism, which allowed it to live at high latitudes in Antarctica.

facts.statement: Vegavis exhibits osteosclerosis, a condition potentially linked to variations in diving behavior.
facts.quote: It also shows a degree of osteosclerosis, a condition shared with Polarornis. This different degrees of osteosclerosis could be related to variations in diving behaviour.

facts.statement: Vegavis iaai is an extinct bird belonging to the family Vegaviidae and is the only known member of the genus Vegavis.
facts.quote: Vegavis iaai es una especie extinta de aves anseriformes de la familia Vegaviidae y único miembro conocido del género Vegavis

facts.statement: Vegavis is most closely related to the modern family Anatidae (ducks and geese) but is not considered a direct ancestor of that family.
facts.quote: Entre las aves modernas, Vegavis está más relacionado con la familia Anatidae (patos y gansos) pero no se considera que sea un ancestro directo de esta

facts.statement: The type specimen of Vegavis iaai, cataloged as MLP 93-I-3-1, was found in deposits at Cape Lamb on Vega Island, Antarctica, in 1992.
facts.quote: El espécimen, catalogado como MLP 93-I-3-1, fue encontrado en depósitos del Cabo Lamb de la Isla Vega, Antártica, en 1992

facts.statement: The species was not described until 2005 because the fossil consists of delicate remains embedded in a concretion that required meticulous preparation.
facts.quote: pero solo fue descrito como una nueva especie en 2005 porque consiste de restos muy delicados de un ave embebida en una concreción

facts.statement: Computed axial tomography scans were used to study the bone structure without risking damage or destruction of the fossils.
facts.quote: Se utilizaron escaneos de tomografía axial computarizada (TAC) para ganar en claridad de imagen de la estructura ósea sin correr peligro de dañar o destruir los huesos

facts.statement: Vegavis iaai lived in Antarctica during the Late Cretaceous (Maastrichtian stage), approximately 65 million years ago.
facts.quote: que vivió durante el Cretácico Superior (estadio Maastrichtiense) de la Antártida, hace unos 65 millones de años

facts.statement: The genus Vegavis lived between 72.2 and 66 million years ago during the Maastrichtian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Maastrichtian to Maastrichtian (72.2 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Vegavis belongs to the parent group Anseriformes.
